name: PT Chandra Daya Investasi TBK.

frontmatter.title: Chandra Daya Investasi: infrastructure earnings wrapped in a financial portfolio, priced for perfection
frontmatter.summary: CDIA is the Prajogo group's listed infrastructure vehicle: electricity distribution in the Krakatau industrial estate, water, tanks and jetties, and a fast-growing vessel fleet. Reported profit is mostly financial income; the operating business is small against the share price. On our DCF the shares sit far above fundamental value, and the konglo lens keeps only part of that premium for twelve months.
thesis: Four infrastructure pillars inside the Chandra Asri group: electricity distribution in the Krakatau industrial estate, water, tank and jetty storage, and marine and land logistics [S4, S5].
FY2025 profit is dominated by non-operating items - fair-value gains and bond income - while the operating business generated a fraction of reported net profit [S4].

A large related-party financial portfolio - equity-linked bonds issued by the parent and a new loan receivable from CAP subsidiaries - sits alongside the operating assets and must be valued separately [S4, S2].
The shares trade far above our DCF value; the premium is a float and regime variable, not an earnings variable [S10, S8].
The free-float deadline inside twelve months is the dated force that should compress part of the premium [S8, S10].

The register is two blocks - CAP at 60.0% and EGCO's Phoenix Power B.V. at 30.0% - leaving about a tenth free-float, so the marginal price is set by float and regime rather than by the operating earnings [S2, S4, S10].

catalysts.event: Third-quarter 2026 results and the first disclosure after the half-year profit decline [S9]
First free-float deadline: large caps with float below the threshold must reach the intermediate step [S8]
End of the MSCI consultation feedback period on Standalone status for Indonesia [S11]
MSCI decision on the Standalone proposal [S11]

blocks.text: Chandra Daya Investasi is the listed infrastructure arm of the Chandra Asri group, itself part of the Barito/Prajogo empire. It runs four businesses - electricity distribution in the Krakatau industrial estate, water treatment, tank and jetty storage, and a marine and land logistics fleet - and it listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in mid-2025 [S4, S5]. We initiate at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp311 against a last price of Rp436, a return of -28.3%.

The variant view is about what the profit is. FY2025 net profit attributable to shareholders was US$121.1m, but operating profit was only US$22.3m; the gap is fair-value gains on financial instruments of US$74.1m, finance income of US$24.3m, and the share of associate profit [S4]. The company is a utility whose reported earnings are largely a treasury result. On our DCF, the operating business plus the financial portfolio is worth Rp97 a share over twelve months, and Rp90 today; the market pays Rp436, which is 4.9x today's fundamental value and more than three times the twelve-month value [S4, S2, S10].

The konglo lens does not assume that premium disappears. It measures the gap and keeps most of it for twelve months: the base regime case closes 35.0% of the log gap, which takes the target to Rp311 - still far above fundamental value, but well below today's price [S2]. That reading is the most likely path for a stock whose marginal price is set by a thin float and a dated regulatory calendar.

Three things move the value from here: whether capex normalises after the fleet build-out, whether the logistics segment integrates at the margins it printed in FY2025, and the free-float deadline in March 2027, which sits five months inside our window [S4, S9, S8].

Industrial-estate utilities sell electricity, water and port services to the tenants of a single estate, usually under long-term contracts. The business is capital-heavy and low-beta, and its value depends on the estate's occupancy and on the pass-through of the state utility's tariff rather than on commodity prices.

CDIA reports three operating segments - energy, logistics, and tank and jetty rental - alongside smaller other services [S4]. Energy is the largest: sales of electricity and other electrical services were US$95.3m of FY2025 revenue of US$148.0m [S4]. The energy pillar runs a gas and steam combined-cycle plant with 120 MW of capacity serving the Krakatau industrial estate, with 311 industrial, commercial, social and government customers and a household customer base on top [S5]. The group also holds an interest in an associate that operates a 200 MW coal-fired plant [S5].

Logistics is the growth engine. Time charter vessel revenue was US$34.6m in FY2025, against US$102.3m of group revenue a year earlier, as the group bought vessels and built a land logistics platform [S4]. Tank and jetty leasing contributed US$5.6m of revenue, and the group commissioned a bitumen tank at Merak in October 2026 [S4, S6]. The four pillars - energy, water, port and storage, and logistics - are managed as one ecosystem for the group's industrial customers [S5].

The customer base is concentrated, and the filing discloses it: two customers each took more than a tenth of FY2025 revenue - CAP at US$16.4m and PT Krakatau Posco at US$15.4m - and related-party sales were 15.7% of revenue [S4]. That concentration is structural: the estate utility sells to the tenants of the estate, and the controlling shareholder's petrochemical complex is one of them.

The controlling shareholder is the Prajogo Pangestu family through the Barito group; CDIA is a subsidiary of Chandra Asri Pacific, which holds 60.0% of the shares [S5, S2]. The register is a two-block structure: Phoenix Power B.V. holds 30.0% (37,448.8m shares) as the non-controlling shareholder, the public holds 10.0%, and directors hold a negligible slice, with no other holder above five per cent [S2, S4, S5]. Phoenix is part of the EGCO Group chain in the annual report's ownership chart, not a Prajogo or Barito affiliate, so the family's controlling block is CAP's 60.0% [S5]. The group's stated strategy is to integrate energy, water, port and logistics capabilities into a single infrastructure platform and to expand regionally [S5]. Management is led by President Director Fransiskus Ruly Aryawan, with Jonathan Kandinata as Finance Director [S0].

The water pillar supplies clean and industrial water and wastewater treatment to the same estate tenants, and the port and storage pillar operates deep-sea jetties, tanks and liquid-bulk storage; the two together are the smaller half of the operating footprint but they are the part most closely tied to the estate's industrial cycle [S5]. The logistics pillar now spans time-charter vessels, ship freight and land transport and warehousing, which is why its revenue can grow faster than the estate businesses it serves [S4, S5].

The revenue mix explains the margin structure. Energy revenue carries the cost of electricity bought from the state utility and resold into the estate, so it is a high-revenue, low-margin pass-through business; logistics and tank rental are capital-intensive but earn materially higher segment margins [S4]. In FY2025 the logistics segment earned a segment result before unallocated costs of US$12.0m, up from US$1.9m a year earlier as the fleet came into service; that is about two-fifths of group EBITDA of US$31.9m [S4].

The company competes in two different markets. In electricity it is the incumbent distributor inside the Krakatau industrial estate, buying bulk power and gas and reselling it to tenants under long-term arrangements [S5]. In logistics and storage it is a challenger in a fragmented Indonesian market, adding vessels and tanks to serve the group's own cargo and third-party industrial flows [S5, S9].

The moat is the estate. An industrial-estate distribution network is a natural monopoly inside its fence: duplicating substations, water treatment and jetty access for a single tenant makes little sense, and the customer relationships are long-dated [S5]. That advantage does not extend into shipping, where charter rates are set by a competitive market and the group is one of many owners.

Five forces, read across the pillars. Buyer power is high in electricity because the estate's anchor tenants are large and can negotiate, and moderate in tank and jetty rental where switching costs are real. Supplier power is high because the state utility supplies the bulk power that CDIA resells, and gas and vessel prices are set externally [S4]. Substitutes are limited inside the estate but real in logistics, where road transport and third-party fleets compete. Rivalry is low in estate distribution and high in shipping. Entry barriers are the estate concession and the capital needed for tanks and vessels - which is also why the group has to keep spending [S4].

The regulation that matters most in the near term is capital-markets regulation, not utility regulation. The exchange has raised the minimum free float and set staged deadlines: large caps with a float below the intermediate threshold must reach it by the end of March 2027 and the full minimum a year later [S8]. OJK has said the rule moves the floor from the old level to the new one and has kept an exit-policy option for companies that cannot comply [S7]. For a stock with a float below a tenth of the register - 9.8% on the exchange-registry mirror - that calendar is a first-order driver of the marginal price [S10, S8].

On utility regulation, the estate distribution business operates under arrangements with the state utility and the industrial tenants rather than under a single national tariff formula, so the relevant test is the renewal and pricing of those arrangements rather than a scheduled tariff review [S5]. The capital cycle is the other industry feature that matters: tanks, jetties and vessels are long-lived assets with lumpy purchase decisions, and the group has chosen to buy scale rather than build it, which makes the acquisition price and the utilisation of the acquired fleet the swing factors in returns [S4, S5].

The sector deck used here is the macro deck only, since the product is domestic electricity, water and logistics rather than a traded commodity [S2]. The relevant macro variables are the rupiah, the policy rate and domestic industrial activity; the group earns in dollars but trades in rupiah, which adds a translation layer to the equity story [S4].

Indonesia's industrial estates typically host captive utilities that supply power, water and port services to tenants under long-term contracts. The estate operator often holds a distribution licence inside the estate and buys bulk power from the state utility, so its margin is a regulated or negotiated spread rather than a generation margin.

Group revenue rose to US$148.0m in FY2025 from US$102.3m in FY2024, driven by the logistics fleet and by energy volumes [S4]. Cost of revenue rose with it to US$112.6m, leaving a gross profit of US$35.4m and a gross margin that recovered from the FY2024 start-up year [S4]. The first half of FY2026 continued the pattern: revenue of US$82.1m, up on the prior year, with logistics revenue growing fastest [S9].

Our EBITDA history is rebuilt from the filing, not from the data pack. The pack's depreciation line captures only part of the charge; the notes show total depreciation of US$9.6m in FY2025 and US$8.6m in FY2024 [S4]. On that basis FY2025 EBITDA was US$31.9m, a margin of 21.6%, and FY2024 EBITDA was US$10.8m [S4].

Management reports a higher EBITDA, and we reconcile it rather than dismiss it. In the first half, reported gross profit of US$19.6m less selling costs of US$0.7m and G&A of US$11.8m leaves operating profit; adding back depreciation of US$9.7m gives our H1 EBITDA. Management's US$31.6m is higher by close to the sum of the items below the operating line - the share of associate profit of US$6.6m, the net foreign-exchange gain of US$10.0m and the other net loss of US$-0.9m - so we read it as EBITDA plus non-operating income, not as a higher operating margin. If that bridge is legitimate, the operating business earns more than we credit it; we do not capitalise an undisclosed definition [S2, S9].

The profit line is where the quality question sits. FY2025 profit before tax was US$132.1m against EBIT of US$22.3m [S4]. The difference is fair-value gains on financial instruments of US$74.1m, bond and deposit interest of US$24.3m, dividend income, foreign-exchange gains and the share of associate profit, partly offset by finance costs of US$28.3m [S4]. None of that is recurring in the way an operating margin is; the first half of FY2026 already showed the unwind, with a much lower net margin than the prior year [S9].

Cash conversion is weak relative to reported profit. Operating cash flow was a small fraction of net profit of US$127.8m, and capex was US$206.4m, of which the logistics segment took the largest share [S4]. The group funds the gap with debt: total debt rose from US$292.9m to US$562.6m and further in the first half of FY2026 [S4, S2].

Net debt is taken on the filing's own cash line, not the data pack's. At 30 June 2026 cash and cash equivalents were US$420.3m against total debt of US$768.0m, so net debt is close to half the gross figure [S2]. The data pack's larger cash figure folds in US$206.8m of listed shares classified at fair value through profit or loss - they are other financial assets, not cash [S2]. We carry those shares as a separate bridge asset at book, so they are counted once and the leverage ratio is not flattered [S2, S0]. The historical cash line behind the summary table is restated to the filing basis as well - FY2025A cash of US$470.1m and FY2024A cash of US$180.2m replace the pack's figures - so net debt and net debt/EBITDA print positive and the FY2025A ratio of 2.9x ties to the December 2025 filing [S4, S2]. The FY2026E column is a year-end roll, not the mid-year position: it does not deduct the first-half deployment into the related-party loan and the listed-share portfolio, which the bridge carries as assets, so it prints less net debt than the 30 June 2026 actual of US$768.0m less US$420.3m; the leverage and cover test in this section is run on the filing position, where net debt is about eight times the FY2026E EBITDA run-rate [S2, S4].

The balance sheet carries a related-party financial portfolio that is larger than the operating asset base in value terms. Investment in other financial assets was US$553.1m at end-FY2025, of which US$326.4m was equity-linked bonds issued by the parent with an annual coupon of 6.8% [S4]. The group also holds US$150.7m of associates and a portfolio of listed shares classified at fair value [S4]. At 30 June 2026 the non-current financial-asset line had grown to US$357.9m, and a new related-party loan receivable of US$238.0m appeared - nil at FY2025 - after US$235.0m was disbursed to CAP subsidiaries in the first half [S2]. We value all of it separately in the bridge rather than letting it flatter the operating multiple, and we carry the loan at a discount to face in the governance section.

Earnings-quality flags: first, the fair-value gain is a mark-to-market result, not cash, and it will reverse if the underlying instruments fall; second, related-party revenue is 15.7% of the total and the largest financial asset is a bond issued by the controlling shareholder's listed vehicle; third, the group's own EBITDA measure is not defined in the filing and is not reconciled to EBIT plus depreciation; fourth, the related-party loan and the parent bond together are the balance sheet's dominant exposure [S4, S9, S2]. The auditor issued an unqualified opinion [S5]. There is no going-concern or late-filing notation in the materials reviewed.

Our forecast holds the last actual's economics: gross margin at 23.5%, operating costs at about 10.0% of revenue, D&A at 11.5%, and revenue growth of 16.0% in FY2026E, fading to 8.0% by FY2030E [S4, S9]. Capex stays at 105.0% of revenue in FY2026E and falls to a steady reinvestment rate above the depreciation rate by the end of the forecast, covering replacement and the terminal growth [S4, S9]. Operating EBIT is taxed at 22.0%, the statutory rate, because the FY2025 group rate reflects non-operating income [S4, S2]. Net borrowing funds the remaining gap [S2].

The FY2026E margin step is the D&A ratio, not revenue. Gross margin is held at 23.5% and operating costs at 10.0%; because depreciation sits inside cost of revenue, the model adds back D&A at 11.5% of revenue against the FY2025 charge of US$9.6m. Holding the post-D&A gross margin constant therefore lifts the ex-D&A margin from the FY2025 ratio to about the H1 2026 print, where gross profit of US$19.6m on revenue of US$82.1m with depreciation of US$9.7m implies an ex-D&A gross margin near the model's. One half-year is the whole evidence: a two-percentage-point lower ex-D&A margin takes the twelve-month base-case value to the low band of the sensitivity table [S2, S4].

Leverage and cover are the test the utility card sets. Gross debt reaches US$768.0m against EBITDA of US$42.9m, and cash interest of US$39.4m exceeds EBIT of US$23.2m - cover below one before any portfolio income [S2, S4]. The debt path restarts from the 30 June 2026 actual; the engine charges interest on the opening 2025 balance, so the first-half annualised run-rate enters the charge from FY2027E, when the restarted base is the opening balance, and cover stays below one [S2]. On the house AFFO definition, take EBITDA of US$42.9m, deduct maintenance capex proxied by D&A of US$19.7m, cash interest of US$39.4m and cash tax of US$7.7m: AFFO is negative, so the operating business does not clear the sovereign-yield hurdle. The equity value rests on the financial portfolio, not on the utility's free cash flow.

The disclosed long-term operating contracts are related-party vessel time charters expiring in 2032, 2037 and 2041 [S2]; the tank and jetty leases and the estate distribution arrangements do not disclose maturities in the notes, which is a disclosure gap we carry as renewal risk rather than a dated cliff.

We value CDIA on a discounted cash flow, with the balance-sheet financial portfolio added through the bridge and the operating business carried at its free cash flow. The method fits because the estate utility and the tank and jetty contracts are long-dated and capital-intensive, the kind of cash flow a DCF prices better than a near-term multiple - and because the reported earnings multiples are distorted by fair-value gains and related-party interest income [S4]. We do not have a domestic peer set with a comparable estate-utility and financial-portfolio mix, so no peer median enters the target; we still show the multiples the market is paying: 116.2x FY2026E earnings, 78.0x EV/EBITDA and an FCFE yield of 2.3% [S0].

The cost of capital is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and an unlevered beta of 0.60, levered to 0.72 at the group's debt-to-equity ratio [S2]. That gives a cost of equity of 9.9% and a WACC of 9.0%. The cost of debt is 7.0%, consistent with the bank pricing disclosed in the notes [S4].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$60.2m for the operating business, with 210.4% of enterprise value in the terminal period - more than the whole EV, because the explicit years are cash-negative while the fleet and tank capex is heavy [S4]. We set terminal capex at replacement plus growth, not replacement alone: the D&A rate of 11.5% plus growth capex consistent with the 2.0% terminal growth, so the terminal reinvestment rate matches the revenue it supports. Replacement-only capex in a growing business would inflate the terminal value, and the DCF table already carries the higher rate [S4]. Adding the non-current financial portfolio, the associates at their filing carrying values, the related-party loan at a discount to face and the listed shares in other current assets at book, and deducting the filing's net debt - the 30 June 2026 position of US$768.0m gross debt less US$420.3m cash, not the forecast roll - and minorities, gives a fundamental value of Rp97 a share over twelve months, against Rp436 in the market [S2, S9]. The KPE associate is carried at US$79.3m, already above its US$55.8m cost including the derivative, so no uplift to the annual report's stated US$200.0m stake worth is supported [S2, S5]. On our reverse DCF the price requires revenue growth of 27.5%, a pace the company has not sustained outside the acquisition year [S9].

The bridge's largest item is the financial portfolio. The US$357.9m of non-current financial assets includes the US$326.4m CAP-issued equity-linked bond, carried at the filing's fair value rather than at par; the note discloses the issuer, the 6.8% coupon and the option over a majority stake in CAP's Cilegon terminal and storage subsidiary, but not a redemption schedule - a transparency gap on the largest bridge item [S4]. A mark the market cannot independently observe deserves a stated sensitivity: haircuts of ten, twenty or thirty per cent reduce the bridge in proportion, and the bear regime case compresses the premium on top of that. We do not apply a haircut in the base because the mark is the audited fair value, and we say so rather than let the reader assume a par carry [S4, S2].

The third bridge item - US$206.8m of listed shares in other current assets, more than a third of bridge equity - is the one mark whose identity we cannot verify. The other-current-assets note says only that it is an investment in shares classified at fair value through profit or loss; the annual report's fair-value hierarchy puts the whole FVTPL equity portfolio at the quoted-price level, so a sibling held inside it would already carry its own konglo premium [S2, S4]. Neither that note, the financial-assets note nor the annual report names the issuers, and none of the Barito/Prajogo listed entities appears in the notes or the annual report as a named investment [S2, S4, S5]. We therefore cannot confirm or exclude a group sibling, and the konglo rule - a covered sibling is marked at its house value, or the parent waits in draft, never at market - cannot be applied name by name. We do not apply a haircut, because that would be an unsourced assumption; instead we bound it. If the entire portfolio were one covered sibling carrying CDIA's own 4.9x premium, stripping that premium would cut the bridge by roughly a fifth and fundamental value by about a quarter, and the SELL would survive. The filing's silence is a disclosure gap we flag, not a mark we can adjust [S2, S4].

The konglo lens then turns fundamental value into the twelve-month target, and it is the lens, not the DCF, that sets most of the number. Today's price is 4.9x our fundamental value today of Rp90 a share - a premium, not a discount - and the lens keeps a probability-weighted share of that premium: over three regime scenarios independent of our business scenarios, the base case closes 35.0% of the log gap, the bear case 75.0% and the bull case -10.0% [S2]. The closing share is raised by the free-float deadline that falls inside the window: the registry float is 9.8% against a next step of 12.5% to be met by March 2027, a gap of 2.7% and 5.0 months away [S10, S8]. The resulting target is Rp311; the base regime scenario alone is Rp273, and the probability-weighted lens is the target [S2].

That the target sits so far above fundamental value is the point, not a comfort. It says the most likely twelve-month price is still a premium to what the assets and cash flows are worth, because a thin float, a family controller and a dated sell-down schedule can keep a premium alive longer than a valuation gap can close it. The bear regime scenario takes the price to Rp145 and the bull regime scenario to Rp556 [S2]. The lens is not a licence to abandon the fundamental work: the DCF is the anchor, and the target is what survives of the premium after the regime step.

The heaviest risk is the ownership regime. The registry float is 9.8% against a minimum that rises in stages, with the first deadline on 31 March 2027 and the full minimum a year later [S10, S8, S7]. The step from the current float to 12.5% is 2.7% of 124,829.4m shares, about three and a half billion shares and roughly one and a half trillion rupiah at Rp436 - about nine weeks of the three-month average daily turnover - so a sell-down would add supply well beyond the market's normal absorption; a failure to sell down would invite the exchange's exit-policy discussion [S7, S10]. Either major holder could supply it: CAP at 60.0% or Phoenix at 30.0%, neither of which needs to cede control at the intermediate step. A placement or rights issue is the alternative remedy and would dilute per-share value; we model no issuance in the base because none has been announced, and we carry it here as a risk [S8, S10]. MSCI's consultation on Standalone status, with the decision due by the end of June 2027, falls inside our twelve-month window and caps any re-rating that depends on index flows [S11]. The stock is not on the exchange's high-concentration list as of late October, so it has not yet suffered the IHSG exclusion - but its float places it squarely inside the rule's target population [S12, S8].

The related-party exposure is the largest single risk on the balance sheet. The US$238.0m loan receivable from CAP subsidiaries is one of the biggest lines on a US$1,933.4m balance sheet; it was nil a year earlier and US$235.0m was disbursed in the first half at a fixed coupon above our 7.0% funding cost, generating US$3.0m of H1 interest income [S2]. The contractual coupon is above our 7.0% funding cost, but the H1 income shows the loan was only partly invested in the period, and the return depends on the borrowers' credit - three unlisted CAP subsidiaries - rather than on the coupon. Governance risk therefore sits on the asset side as well as in the revenue line [S2].

Operationally, energy revenue depends on the estate's tenants and on the state utility's tariff; a pass-through squeeze compresses the largest segment's margin [S4]. Logistics depends on charter rates and vessel utilisation, and the fleet was bought at a cyclical moment; a softening charter market would hit the segment that drove FY2025 growth [S4, S9]. Leverage is rising: debt increased again in the first half of FY2026 while capex stayed heavy [S2].

The honest bull case is strategic, not operating. The group has options we do not put in the base: CAP holds 60.0% and has an incentive to use CDIA as its listed infrastructure vehicle, while Phoenix's 30.0% EGCO stake gives it a partner with the same interest in a liquid, index-eligible vehicle; the KPE associate stake (200 MW of coal-fired capacity, carried at US$79.3m) and the estate expansion give the group assets to inject or grow; an asset injection or a placement to either major holder would also fix the float without a controller sale; and index re-inclusion would follow a repaired float [S5, S8, S10]. None of that is announced, so it is a scenario, not a forecast; it is the main reason the bull regime target sits at Rp556 [S2].

Currency and governance are secondary but real. The group reports in dollars and trades in rupiah, and the rupiah path is a macro input the company does not control [S2]. Related-party revenue and the related-party bond portfolio concentrate governance risk in the controlling shareholder, and the portfolio's fair value is a mark that the market cannot independently observe [S4].

Business scenarios and regime scenarios are separate. Our business scenarios - bear, base and bull with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25%, which sum to one - drive fundamental value: the bear case takes fundamental value to Rp66 and the bull case to Rp142 [S2]. The weights are set in the assumptions as a quarter, a half and a quarter; a rendering that shows them as one-decimal fractions is rounding the quarters and does not change the total. The bear case assumes softer charter rates after the fleet expansion, revenue growth halving and gross margin compression while capex stays high; the bull case assumes faster integration, firm utilisation and an earlier capex normalisation [S4, S9].

The konglo lens is the second layer, and it must be read with the business scenarios rather than instead of them. Because the price is a premium to fundamental value, the lens works to keep part of the gap rather than to close it: the base regime scenario closes 35.0% of the log gap and takes fundamental value of Rp97 to a target of Rp311 [S2]. The flags that raise the closing share are the free-float deadline inside the window and any enforcement action; the high-concentration listing is not in the registry today, so the compression is driven by the float calendar rather than by a forced index exit [S2, S8]. A premium that is not compressed fast enough is the central risk to our target, and the bull regime scenario - where the premium re-expands - is the honest upside case [S2].

Signposts that would change the view: a controller sell-down or a placement that lifts the float toward the intermediate threshold; the March 2027 free-float review; the MSCI decision; a material related-party transaction at the group level; and the capex and charter-rate path in the quarterly releases [S8, S2, S4].

CDIA is a Prajogo Pangestu family-controlled company, a subsidiary of Chandra Asri Pacific within the Barito group. The register is two blocks, not one: CAP holds 60.0%, Phoenix Power B.V. holds 30.0% (37,448.8m shares), directors hold a negligible slice and the public holds 10.0%, with no other holder above five per cent [S2, S4, S5]. Phoenix is a related party - the notes name it as the non-controlling shareholder [S4] - but it is not a Prajogo affiliate: the annual report's ownership chart places it in the EGCO Group chain (EGCO Plus and New Growth Plus B.V.), and the two major shareholders are CAP and Thailand's EGCO Group [S5]. The family's controlling block is therefore CAP's 60.0%, not the ninety per cent that the data pack's insider line implies; that line adds the EGCO stake to the family's and is not used here. The exchange-registry float is 9.8%, a fraction of a point below the audited public block [S10, S4]. The controller's 60.0% still sits far above the level at which a float-driven market can price the business on fundamentals, which is why the konglo lens rather than the DCF sets the twelve-month target [S2].

The free-float rule is the governance event of the next eighteen months. The exchange requires large caps below the intermediate threshold to reach it by 31 March 2027 and the full minimum by 31 March 2028, and OJK has retained an exit-policy option for companies that do not comply [S8, S7]. CDIA does not appear on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list as of 22 October 2026, and no index deletion or enforcement action is recorded against it [S12]. That is a status, not an absolution: the float is below the intermediate threshold and the deadline is inside our forecast window [S10, S8].

Related-party gravity is the central governance question, and it is now two-sided. Related-party sales were 15.7% of FY2025 revenue [S4]. The group holds US$326.4m of equity-linked bonds issued by the parent with a coupon of 6.8%, plus bonds and listed shares, and the largest single financial asset is therefore a claim on the controlling shareholder's other listed vehicle [S4]. On the asset side it also carries the US$238.0m loan receivable from three CAP subsidiaries - Aster Power, Aster Port & Terminals and Chandra Asri Capital - nil at FY2025, with US$235.0m disbursed in the first half at a fixed coupon above our funding cost, long-dated maturities, and only US$3.0m of H1 interest income [S2]. Together the loan and the parent bond are just under a third of a US$1,933.4m balance sheet, and we carry the loan at four-fifths of face in the bridge for related-party credit and observability. These are disclosed and valued at fair value, so they are optics-class rather than manipulation-class flags - but they mean the balance sheet's quality depends on the parent's credit and on marks the market cannot verify [S4, S2]. The US$206.8m quoted listed-share portfolio is the third asset in that family: it is quoted, so the mark is observable, but the filing does not name the issuers, so we cannot confirm that it holds no Barito/Prajogo sibling. We flag that disclosure gap in the valuation section rather than adjust the mark without a source [S2, S4].

The dividend record is thin relative to the capital programme: dividends paid were US$20.0m in FY2025 against parent profit of US$121.1m, and the group is retaining cash for the fleet and tank build-out [S4]. The auditor is Liana Ramon Xenia & Rekan, which issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 statements [S5]. The board and management are disclosed in the annual report, with the President Director and Finance Director named [S0, S5].

ESG exposures are concentrated in the energy pillar - gas-fired generation, emissions and process safety at the combined-cycle plant - and in the estate's water and wastewater operations [S5]. The logistics fleet adds fuel and emissions exposure, and the group's own reporting highlights solar capacity additions as its decarbonisation lever [S5].

The dated regime calendar dominates: the March 2027 free-float step, the end of the MSCI consultation feedback period in April 2027 and the MSCI decision by the end of June 2027 [S8, S11]. Group corporate actions - a controller sell-down, a placement or a related-party asset transfer - are the other dated catalysts, and the October 2026 bitumen tank commissioning and offshore vessel launch show the operating expansion is still running [S6].

On the operating side we monitor the quarterly revenue mix between energy and logistics, the charter utilisation behind the time-charter line, the energy segment's pass-through margin, and capex against the depreciation charge [S4, S9]. The key test is whether capex falls toward the D&A rate as management says the fleet build-out completes; until it does, free cash flow stays negative and the DCF's terminal value carries the valuation [S4].

Between updates the KPIs are: revenue growth and segment mix, EBITDA after the restated depreciation charge, the fair-value result on the financial portfolio, net debt and the cost of debt, the free float against the regulatory step, and any change in the controller's effective stake [S2, S4, S8]. The fair-value line is the one to watch for earnings quality: a reversal would remove the largest single contributor to FY2025 profit [S4].

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the first half (+22.8% year on year, S9), with logistics revenue up 80.2% on fleet additions and energy up 5.4%; growth then fades as the acquired fleet annualises, to 12%, 10%, 9% and 8% before a 5% long-run rate. No volume decline is assumed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 23.9% and the first half of FY2026 also 23.9% (S4, S9); the 2024 trough reflected start-up costs in the new vessel business. Held at the last actual, no default haircut.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling plus G&A was 8.8% of revenue (S4). The first half of FY2026 carried 6.9m of professional fees (S2) that we treat as non-recurring; we normalise to 10.0% and ease to 9.5%, above the FY2025 level to allow for a listed-company cost base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the filing: FY2025 depreciation was 9.62m (S4, F1) and the first half of FY2026 alone 9.67m (S2) as the acquired vessels entered service, so D&A steps up to about 11.5% of revenue and stays there with the larger asset base.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was 206m, or 139% of revenue, mostly the logistics fleet and tank additions (S4, F11); the first half of FY2026 spent 94.2m (S9). We model the build-out continuing at about one times revenue in FY2026 and then fading to a steady reinvestment rate: replacement at the D&A rate of 11.5% of revenue plus growth capex of about 2pp for the 2% terminal growth, so the long-run rate is 13.5% rather than replacement-only. A perpetual one-times-revenue capex would value the assets at zero.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 4.7% of revenue and 1.2% at 30 June 2026 (S4, S2); held at 5% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate on operating profit
assumptions.basis: Operating EBIT is taxed at the 22% statutory rate the engine also uses in the WACC. The FY2025 3.2% group effective rate is an artefact of FVTPL gains, bond income taxed at source and equity-accounted associate income, none of which sit in operating EBIT (S4). H1 2026 tax was 8.31m on profit before tax of 27.63m, a 30% effective rate (S2), so 22% is not a cautious choice.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense on bank loans and leases was 28.25m on debt of 562.6m (S4), and the first half of FY2026 ran at 22.4m; we use 7.0%, consistent with the marginal bank pricing in Note 17.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income was 24.3m, including 8.6m of bond coupons and 12.4m of deposit and current account interest (S4); on the reported cash balance that is about 4-5%, which we hold.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The path restarts from the 30 June 2026 actual: debt rose from 562.6m at December 2025 to 767.986m by June 2026 (S4, S2), a 205.4m first-half increase, so FY2026E adds that actual increase rather than 150m; we then assume 100m in FY2027 and 50m in FY2028, then no net new debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Recurring non-operating income is the coupon and fair-value income on the 553m bond portfolio and the 12.4m share of associate profit (S4); the 74.1m FVTPL gain in FY2025 is not repeated. We carry 30m a year, falling to 25m in perpetuity as bonds mature.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 6.74m of FY2025 net profit of 127.79m, or 5.3% (S4); held at 5.5%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividends paid were 20.0m against prior-year parent profit of 31.4m (S4); with capex still heavy we assume a 25% payout of current-year parent earnings.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share issuance is assumed in the base: the free-float rule and the registry float are sourced (S8, S10), but the company has not announced whether its remedy will be a controller sell-down, a placement or a rights issue. We treat the placement/rights route as a dilution risk in section 5 rather than a base input, and the IPO shares are already in the share count (S4).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Indonesian long-run nominal growth; the house terminal growth for a rupiah-reporting, dollar-earning infrastructure operator.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA margin is 25.0% against FY2025A 21.6% - the qc calibration gap of 3.43pp - and it is unanswered in qc_justifications. The lift is not operating: EBITDA = gross profit - opex + D&A, the model raises D&A from 9.62m (6.5% of revenue) to 19.75m (11.5%) and adds it back while holding the post-D&A gross margin at 23.5%, so the model implicitly assumes the ex-D&A gross margin rises from 30.4% to 35.0% and stays for 20 years. H1 2026 does show it (revenue 82.146m, gross profit 19.639m = 23.9% post-D&A with D&A 9.674m, i.e. 35.7% ex-D&A; S2 p.6, p.61), but one half-year is the whole evidence and the gate is unanswered. This is optimism against the SELL, not toward it.
challenges.answer: The calibration gap is 3.43pp, below the engine's 5pp BLOCK threshold, so there is no flag to attach a qc_justification to (adding one would orphan it). Instead section 3 states the step is the D&A ratio, not revenue, and quotes H1 gross profit 19.64m on revenue 82.15m with D&A 9.67m (S2 p.6, p.61) to support the ex-D&A margin, and points to the engine's gross-margin -2pp sensitivity cell. The higher tax and terminal capex cut the DCF, so the remaining gap is not value-inflating.

challenges.challenge: tax_rate 5% is applied to operating EBIT in FCFF (fcff = ebit*(1-tax) + da - capex - dnwc) although the 3.2% FY2025 effective rate the basis cites is an artefact of FVTPL gains, bond income taxed at source and equity-accounted income - none of which are in EBIT. The engine's own WACC uses the 22% statutory rate. On operating EBIT of 23.2m (FY2026E) rising to 72.5m (FY2045E), the missing ~17pp of tax is ~15-20% of terminal FCFF and some Rp5-6/share of fundamental. The basis misapplies the LK's group effective rate to an operating base.
challenges.answer: tax_rate changed from 5% to 22% for every forecast year; the basis now says operating EBIT is taxed at the statutory rate the WACC uses, that the FY2025 3.2% group rate reflects FVTPL gains, bond income taxed at source and associate income outside EBIT [S4], and that H1 2026 tax of 8.31m on PBT of 27.63m is a 30% effective rate [S2]. Engine rerun and fundamental restated.

challenges.challenge: Terminal capex is set at 12% of revenue, equal to the D&A rate, while revenue still grows 5% to FY2045 and 2% in perpetuity, and 85.1% of the DCF value is in the terminal period. Replacement-only capex in a growing business mechanically inflates the terminal value; the POWER_UTILITIES card treats utilities as a bond with growth options, which requires the terminal reinvestment rate to be consistent with terminal growth.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex raised from 12% to 13.5% of revenue - replacement at the 11.5% D&A rate plus about 2pp of growth capex for the 2% terminal growth - and the basis and section 4 now disclose the reinvestment consistency; the capex fade ends above D&A rather than at it, and the drift justification is updated.

challenges.challenge: The POWER_UTILITIES card requires an AFFO yield vs 10y FR, net debt/EBITDA, interest cover, contract length/escalators and anchor-customer percentage. None is in sections 4-5. The numbers matter: gross debt 768.0m is 17.9x FY2026E EBITDA, H1 finance cost 22.4m (~44.8m/yr) exceeds EBIT of 23.2m, so on the house AFFO definition (EBITDA - maintenance capex - cash interest - cash tax) AFFO is negative and fails the 10y FR hurdle without the portfolio income. The claim that multiples are unavailable is overstated: the engine produces FY2026E PE 61.3x, EV/EBITDA 67.3x and FCFE yield 1.27%, and BREN.JK is a computable same-industry peer.
challenges.answer: Added an AFFO bridge and cover test in section 3: FY2026E EBITDA less D&A-proxy maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax is negative, and cash interest exceeds EBIT. Section 4 now shows the FY2026E PE, EV/EBITDA and FCFE yield even though no peer median exists. challenges.challenge: The US$326.4m equity-linked bonds (6.8% coupon, issued by the parent CAP) are carried at 100% of the 357.9m bridge mark - 61% of the DCF-derived equity value - while the report itself says the mark is one "the market cannot independently observe". In a regime where the group's listed names are 80-89% below their peaks and CAP/TPIA was deleted from MSCI, an equity-linked parent bond is the most mark-exposed asset on the balance sheet, and the FY2025 74.1m FVTPL gain has already gone (H1 2026 FVTPL gain nil, other -0.85m, S2 Note 27).
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the ELB is a CAP-issued instrument with a 6.8% coupon and an option over a majority of CAP's Cilegon terminal subsidiary, and that the note gives no redemption schedule [S4]; it is carried at the filing's fair value (not par), and discloses a ten/twenty/thirty per cent haircut sensitivity; the bear regime case compresses the premium on top. The 12.5% step needs 2.73% of 124.75bn shares, ~3.41bn shares or ~Rp1.5tn at Rp436, against ADTV of Rp33.8bn (about 44 days of turnover); the report never sizes the supply.

challenges.challenge: The bridge carries US$206.8m of "other financial assets - investment in shares classified as FVTPL" at 30 June 2026, described in the report as "listed shares at FVTPL (Note 7), carried at book". That is 36% of the US$571.9m bridge equity value, and the fair-value hierarchy puts the shares at Level 1, quoted prices (S4 p.116). The filing does not name the issuers and the report neither identifies the portfolio nor states that it contains no Barito/Prajogo listed sibling. VAL_KONGLO_REGIME §4 requires parent and siblings to agree on each other's marks; a covered sibling marked at market inside a holding structure is a RETURN, and BREN is covered (revision, no approved house value) while BRPT/TPIA have no house model.
challenges.answer: Searched the H1 other-current-assets note and financial-assets note (S2), the FY2025 audited notes and fair-value hierarchy (S4) and the annual report (S5). The US$206.8m is an FVTPL investment in shares; the annual report's hierarchy puts the whole FVTPL equity portfolio at the quoted-price level; no issuer is named in any of the three documents and no Barito/Prajogo entity appears as a named investment. Added an explicit statement in section 4 and a flag in section 6: the filing does not disclose the issuers, so a covered sibling can be neither confirmed nor excluded and the konglo sibling rule cannot be applied name by name. The mark stays at quoted fair value - no unsourced haircut - with the bound quantified: if the entire portfolio were one covered sibling carrying CDIA's 4.87x premium, stripping it would remove about a fifth of the bridge and a quarter of fundamental value, and the SELL survives. The assumptions bridge label now says the same so the table cannot imply a verified portfolio.

findings.finding: The FY2026E-FY2030E net-debt line is rolled from net new borrowing (205.4m / 100m / 50m) and ignores the negative FCFF it reports in the same table (-144.0m, -102.6m, -59.3m), so forecast net debt rises by 195.4m / 111.1m / 71.6m while the cash flow implies a much larger increase. The FY2026E roll also opens from the December 2025 net debt of 92.5m and adds the H1 debt increase, but not the H1 cash decline from the 238.0m related-party loan and the 206.8m listed share purchases, so it prints 287.9m net debt / 6.7x against the 30 June 2026 actual 347.7m / 8.1x stated in the same section [S2, S4]. The valuation is unaffected (the DCF and bridge use the 347.7m filing position) but the forecast leverage table understates the leverage path.

Section 4 says no uplift to the KPE associate is supported because the US$79.3m carrying value is "already above its US$55.8m cost including the derivative", against the annual report's US$200m 'worth' for the 45% stake [S5 p.58]. The rebuttal is incomplete: S2 p.62 shows the US$55.8m is the cost of the additional 29,085,000 shares (35%) including a US$9.38m derivative, not the total 45% cost, so the report does not actually address the US$200m statement from S5. The associate line is US$172.8m, 30% of bridge equity. The refusal is conservative and the SELL survives, but the sentence overstates its evidential basis.

The US$238.0m related-party loan receivable is carried at 80% of face (probability 0.8 in valuation.bridge), a US$47.6m haircut, about Rp7/share, on a performing 12%-coupon loan with maturities 2030-2035 to three CAP subsidiaries [S2 p.88 / F24]. No source supports a 20% loss-given-default, and the method card forbids default haircuts unless sourced.

The business scenarios are numerically mirrored (+/-4pp revenue growth, +/-2pp gross margin, 25/50/25), but both narratives promise a capex divergence that is not modelled: the bear case says "capex stays high" and the bull case "capex normalises sooner", while capex is identical in all three runs. The bear narrative also says revenue growth "halves" when the shock is -4pp (16% to 12%) [fund record scenarios].

The 49% stake in Petrosea Services Solutions Pte Ltd (US$15.5m invested 23 April 2026, carried at US$16.1m) is correctly inside the US$172.8m associates line and covered in post_bs_review [S2 Note 10], but it is not named in sections 1, 3 or 4. A new third-party JV associate acquired in the period should be visible to the reader.

The US$206.8m Level-1 listed-share portfolio remains unidentified after the S2, S4 and S5 searches, and the report now bounds it: stripping a konglo premium would cut the bridge by about a fifth and fundamental value by about a quarter, leaving the SELL intact [fund record section 4]. That satisfies the konglo sibling rule on disclosure. If the FVTPL schedule or annual report lists the issuers, naming them would remove the residual risk of a covered Barito sibling marked at market.
